1-1.title: Time, Timelines, and Eras
1-1.learn:
KEY IDEAS — MEASURING TIME IN HISTORY

Historians put events in order from oldest to newest. A timeline is a line that shows events in the order they happened, with the earliest events on the left and the latest on the right. Putting events in order is called chronological order, or sequencing.

Time words help us talk about big amounts of time. A decade is 10 years, a century is 100 years, and a millennium is 1,000 years. So the years 2000 to 2100 make up one century, and 1,000 years make up a millennium.

Historians also split time into two big eras. 'BC' (before Christ) or 'BCE' (before the common era) counts the years BACKWARD before the year zero — so a bigger BC number is actually further in the PAST. 'AD' or 'CE' counts the years FORWARD after the year zero. Because of this, the year 500 BC happened LONG BEFORE the year 500 AD. When you read BC dates, remember the numbers count down toward zero as time moves forward.

questions.question: What is a timeline used for?

choices.A: To list the rulers of one country only
choices.B: To measure the temperature of the past
choices.C: To draw a map of an ancient city
choices.D: To show events in the order they happened

questions.explanation: A timeline places events in chronological order, from oldest to newest.

questions.question: How many years are in a century?
questions.explanation: A century is 100 years; a decade is 10 and a millennium is 1,000.

questions.question: How many years are in a millennium?
questions.explanation: A millennium equals 1,000 years.

questions.question: Which event happened first, earlier in time?

choices.C: They happened at the same time

questions.explanation: BC dates count backward and come before AD dates, so 500 BC happened long before 500 AD.

questions.question: What does 'BC' (or 'BCE') tell you about a date?

choices.A: It comes after the year zero
choices.B: It comes before the year zero
choices.C: It means the date is unknown
choices.D: It means the date is in the future

questions.explanation: BC/BCE marks years before the year zero, counted backward.

questions.question: On a standard timeline, where are the EARLIEST events placed?
questions.explanation: Timelines run oldest-to-newest left to right, so earliest events sit on the left.

questions.question: Putting events in the order they happened is called what?
questions.explanation: Ordering events by time is called chronological order, or sequencing.

questions.question: Which of these is the LONGEST amount of time?
questions.explanation: A millennium (1,000 years) is longer than a century (100) or decade (10).

questions.question: Among BC dates, which year is the EARLIEST (furthest in the past)?
questions.explanation: BC numbers count backward, so the larger the BC number, the further in the past — 1000 BC is earliest.

questions.question: A historian says an event happened 'two centuries ago.' About how many years is that?
questions.explanation: One century is 100 years, so two centuries is 200 years.

questions.question: How many years are in a decade?
questions.explanation: A decade is 10 years.

questions.question: What does 'AD' (or 'CE') tell you about a date?

choices.A: It comes before the year zero
choices.B: It counts the years forward after the year zero
choices.C: It means the date is unknown
choices.D: It means thousands of years ago

questions.explanation: AD/CE counts the years forward after the year zero.

questions.question: Which of these is the SHORTEST amount of time?
questions.explanation: A year is shorter than a decade, a century, or a millennium.

questions.question: Another word for putting events in chronological order is what?
questions.explanation: Putting events in the order they happened is also called sequencing.

questions.question: Which year happened EARLIER, further in the past?
questions.explanation: BC dates come before AD dates, so 200 BC happened earlier than any of the AD years.

questions.question: On a timeline, where are the most RECENT events placed?
questions.explanation: Timelines run oldest-to-newest from left to right, so the latest events sit on the right.

questions.question: The years 1900 to 2000 make up how much time?
questions.explanation: From 1900 to 2000 is 100 years, which is one century.

questions.question: Which BC year is the MOST RECENT (closest to the year zero)?
questions.explanation: BC numbers count backward, so the smallest BC number is closest to zero — 40 BC is most recent.

questions.question: Five decades equal how many years?
questions.explanation: One decade is 10 years, so five decades is 50 years.

questions.question: Why is the year 300 BC further in the past than the year 100 BC?

choices.A: Because 300 is bigger and BC numbers count backward
choices.D: Because they are the same year

questions.explanation: BC numbers count backward toward zero, so the larger number, 300 BC, is further in the past.

questions.question: How many years are between 100 AD and 400 AD?
questions.explanation: From 100 AD to 400 AD is 300 years.

questions.question: Which list is in correct chronological order, from earliest to latest?
questions.explanation: Earliest to latest runs 500 BC, then 100 AD, then 200 AD.

questions.question: A 'millennium' is best described as how many centuries?
questions.explanation: A millennium is 1,000 years, and since a century is 100 years, that equals 10 centuries.

questions.question: Which abbreviation means the same thing as 'BC'?
questions.explanation: BCE (before the common era) means the same thing as BC.

questions.question: Which abbreviation means the same thing as 'AD'?
questions.explanation: CE (common era) means the same thing as AD.

questions.question: A pyramid built in 2500 BC and a temple built in 500 BC — which was built FIRST?

choices.C: They were built at the same time

questions.explanation: Larger BC numbers are further in the past, so the pyramid built in 2500 BC came first.

questions.question: Which is NOT a unit historians use to measure long periods of time?
questions.explanation: A kilometer measures distance, not time; decade, century, and millennium measure time.

questions.question: If an event happened about 'three decades ago,' roughly how many years is that?
questions.explanation: One decade is 10 years, so three decades is about 30 years.

questions.question: Why is a timeline a helpful tool for studying history?

choices.A: It tells you the weather long ago
choices.B: It lists the prices of ancient goods
choices.D: It shows the order and spacing of events over time

questions.explanation: A timeline shows events in order and how much time passed between them.

questions.question: Which year is closest to today?
questions.explanation: AD years come after BC years and larger AD numbers are more recent, so 2000 AD is closest to today.

questions.question: An era is BEST described as what?

choices.D: A large period of time in history

questions.explanation: An era is a large stretch of time, such as the period before or after the year zero.

questions.question: A coin reads '50 BC' and a statue reads '50 AD.' How far apart in time were they made?
questions.explanation: From 50 BC to 50 AD is about 100 years, since BC and AD count outward from zero.

questions.question: Which sentence about timelines is TRUE?

choices.A: Newest events go on the far left
choices.C: Earliest events go on the left and later ones to the right
choices.D: Events are placed in alphabetical order

questions.explanation: On a timeline, earliest events go on the left and later events to the right.

questions.question: Ten centuries added together equal what?
questions.explanation: Ten centuries is 1,000 years, which equals one millennium.

questions.question: Which event is the EARLIEST?
questions.explanation: The largest BC date is furthest in the past, so the city founded in 753 BC is earliest.

questions.question: Why do historians divide history into eras like BC and AD?

choices.A: To make the past harder to study
choices.B: To organize long stretches of time so events are easier to place
choices.D: Because all events happened in one year

questions.explanation: Dividing time into eras helps historians organize and place events across long periods.

questions.question: Half of a century is how many years?
questions.explanation: A century is 100 years, so half of a century is 50 years.

questions.question: Which pair of dates is exactly one millennium apart?
questions.explanation: From 500 AD to 1500 AD is 1,000 years, which is one millennium.

questions.question: A student lists events as: invention of writing, building of the pyramids, fall of Rome. To make a timeline, the student should arrange them how?

choices.A: By how interesting each one is
choices.B: By how long each event's name is
choices.C: In chronological order, earliest to latest
choices.D: In a circle with no order

questions.explanation: Events on a timeline are arranged in chronological order, earliest to latest.

questions.question: Which statement correctly compares the units of time from shortest to longest?
questions.explanation: From shortest to longest the order is decade (10), century (100), millennium (1,000).

1-2.title: Primary and Secondary Sources
1-2.learn:
KEY IDEAS — PRIMARY VS. SECONDARY SOURCES

Historians study the past using clues called sources. There are two main kinds. A primary source comes straight from the time and place being studied. Examples include a diary written by someone who lived then, a clay tablet, an old letter, a photograph, a speech, or an ancient coin. Primary sources give the most direct evidence about the past because they were made by people who were actually there.

A secondary source is created LATER by someone who studied the primary sources. Examples include a history textbook, a museum sign, an encyclopedia article, or a biography written today about an ancient king. Secondary sources are useful because they explain and organize information, but they are one step removed from the event.

Historians use both. They often start with primary sources for direct evidence, then read secondary sources to understand what experts think it all means. Knowing the difference helps you judge how trustworthy a source is and how close it is to the actual events.

questions.question: Which of these is a PRIMARY source?

choices.A: An encyclopedia article about the war
choices.B: A textbook written 100 years after the war
choices.C: A museum sign describing the war
choices.D: A diary written by a soldier during the war

questions.explanation: A diary from the time of the event is a firsthand, primary source.

questions.question: Which of these is a SECONDARY source?

choices.B: A modern textbook about ancient Sumer
choices.D: A letter written by a Sumerian trader

questions.explanation: A modern textbook was made later by people studying the past, so it is secondary.

questions.question: Why do historians value primary sources?

choices.A: They are always easier to read
choices.B: They are written by modern experts
choices.C: They give the most direct evidence from the time studied

questions.explanation: Primary sources come straight from the time, giving the most direct evidence.

questions.question: An old coin from ancient Rome is an example of what?
questions.explanation: An object made during the time being studied, like a coin, is a primary source.

questions.question: What makes a secondary source different from a primary source?

choices.B: It is created later by someone studying the past
choices.D: It comes directly from the event

questions.explanation: Secondary sources are made later by people who studied primary evidence.

questions.question: A student writes a biography today about an ancient pharaoh. The biography is what kind of source?
questions.explanation: Written long after the events by someone studying them, it is a secondary source.

questions.question: Which list contains ONLY primary sources?

choices.A: A biography, a letter, a website
choices.B: A textbook, a diary, a coin
choices.C: A museum sign, an encyclopedia, a tablet
choices.D: A diary, a clay tablet, an old letter

questions.explanation: A diary, a clay tablet, and an old letter are all firsthand items from the past.

questions.question: Why might a historian use BOTH primary and secondary sources?

choices.A: Primary gives direct evidence; secondary helps explain its meaning
choices.B: Secondary sources are always more accurate
choices.D: Both kinds are exactly the same

questions.explanation: Primary sources give direct evidence, while secondary sources help interpret and organize it.

questions.question: A museum display sign explaining an exhibit is BEST described as what?
questions.explanation: The sign was written later by museum staff who studied the objects, so it is secondary.

questions.question: Which question would BEST help a student decide if a source is primary?

choices.A: Is the source written in English?
choices.B: Was it made by someone present at the time of the event?
choices.C: Is the source long or short?

questions.explanation: Primary sources are made by people present during the time being studied.

questions.question: What is a 'source' in the study of history?

choices.A: A clue used to learn about the past

questions.explanation: A source is a clue, such as an object or a document, used to learn about the past.

questions.question: A photograph taken during an ancient festival would be what kind of source?
questions.explanation: A photograph made at the time of the event is a firsthand, primary source.

questions.question: An encyclopedia article written today about ancient Egypt is what kind of source?
questions.explanation: An encyclopedia article written later by people studying the past is a secondary source.

questions.question: Which of these is a primary source?

choices.A: A documentary film made last year
choices.B: A modern map of the ancient world
choices.D: A speech written and given by an ancient leader

questions.explanation: A speech written and delivered by someone who lived then is a firsthand, primary source.

questions.question: Why is a primary source considered 'closer' to an event than a secondary source?

choices.A: It was made by someone there at the time
choices.B: It is always printed in color
choices.D: It was written many years afterward

questions.explanation: A primary source was made by someone present at the time, so it is closer to the event.

questions.question: A clay tablet with writing pressed into it by an ancient scribe is an example of what?
questions.explanation: An object created during the time being studied, like a clay tablet, is a primary source.

questions.question: Which list contains ONLY secondary sources?

choices.A: A diary, a coin, a letter
choices.B: A tablet, a speech, a photograph
choices.C: A textbook, an encyclopedia, a modern biography
choices.D: A letter, a textbook, a coin

questions.explanation: A textbook, an encyclopedia, and a modern biography were all made later by people studying the past.

questions.question: A historian wants the most direct evidence about how a Roman soldier felt in battle. What is the BEST source?

choices.A: A movie made about Rome last year
choices.B: A modern textbook chapter on Rome
choices.C: An encyclopedia entry on the Roman army
choices.D: A letter the soldier wrote home during the war

questions.explanation: A letter the soldier wrote during the war is a primary source giving the most direct evidence.

questions.question: How does a secondary source help a historian?

choices.A: It explains and organizes information from primary sources
choices.B: It is always written by an eyewitness
choices.C: It is the only kind of source worth using
choices.D: It comes directly from the moment of the event

questions.explanation: Secondary sources explain and organize information gathered from primary sources.

questions.question: Which of these is NOT a primary source?

choices.C: A letter from a person who was there

questions.explanation: An encyclopedia written this year is a secondary source, not a firsthand primary one.

questions.question: A historian usually begins research with primary sources because they provide what?

choices.A: Direct evidence from the time being studied
choices.D: A summary of what experts think

questions.explanation: Primary sources give direct evidence from the time being studied.

questions.question: A painting created by an artist who watched an ancient battle is what kind of source?
questions.explanation: A painting made by someone who witnessed the event is a firsthand, primary source.

questions.question: Which question best tells you a source is SECONDARY?

choices.A: Was it made during the event by someone present?
choices.C: Was it made later by someone who studied the event?

questions.explanation: A secondary source is made later by someone who studied the event.

questions.question: A museum places an ancient sword in a glass case. The sword itself is what kind of source?
questions.explanation: The sword is an object made during the time being studied, so it is a primary source.

questions.question: Why should a historian think about whether a source is primary or secondary?

choices.A: It helps judge how trustworthy and how close to the event the source is
choices.B: It tells how many pages the source has
choices.C: It shows the price of the source
choices.D: It does not matter at all

questions.explanation: Knowing the type helps judge how trustworthy and how close to the event a source is.

questions.question: A modern author writes a book about a queen who lived 2,000 years ago, using old letters and coins. The author's book is what kind of source?
questions.explanation: A book written today using older evidence is a secondary source.

questions.question: Which pairing correctly matches a source to its type?

choices.A: Ancient coin = secondary; modern textbook = primary
choices.B: Ancient coin = primary; modern textbook = secondary

questions.explanation: An ancient coin is a primary source and a modern textbook is a secondary source.

questions.question: A speech recorded by a person who lived 2,500 years ago is valuable to historians mainly because it is what?
questions.explanation: The speech is firsthand evidence from that time, making it a valuable primary source.

questions.question: Which of the following is a secondary source?

choices.A: A traveler's journal from an ancient trip
choices.B: An old map drawn during a voyage
choices.C: A documentary made this year about ancient trade
choices.D: A merchant's receipt from long ago

questions.explanation: A documentary made this year was created later by people studying the past, so it is secondary.

questions.question: What is one weakness of relying ONLY on a secondary source?

choices.A: It is one step removed from the actual event
choices.C: It is always written in another language
choices.D: It cannot be trusted at all

questions.explanation: A secondary source is one step removed from the event because it was made later.

questions.question: A handwritten recipe from an ancient cook is what kind of source?
questions.explanation: A recipe written by someone who lived then is a firsthand, primary source.

questions.question: Which is the BEST example of using both kinds of sources together?

choices.B: Looking only at an ancient coin
choices.C: Studying an ancient letter, then reading a modern book that explains it

questions.explanation: Studying a primary letter and then a secondary book that explains it uses both kinds together.

questions.question: An ancient pot with painted scenes of daily life is useful to historians as what?

choices.A: A secondary source about modern life
choices.B: A primary source showing how people lived then

questions.explanation: The pot was made then and shows life at the time, so it is a primary source.

questions.question: Which is NOT a secondary source?

choices.D: A diary written during the event

questions.explanation: A diary written during the event is a primary source, not a secondary one.

questions.question: A student finds an old letter and a modern article about the same ancient king. Which is the primary source?

choices.A: The old letter from that time

questions.explanation: The old letter from that time is the primary source; the modern article is secondary.

questions.question: Why are secondary sources still useful even though they are not firsthand?

choices.A: They are always older than primary sources
choices.B: They help explain and make sense of the evidence
choices.C: They were made during the event

questions.explanation: Secondary sources help explain and organize the evidence found in primary sources.

questions.question: Which of these would be a primary source for studying an ancient flood?

choices.C: A clay tablet written by someone who survived the flood

questions.explanation: A tablet written by a survivor of the flood is firsthand evidence, a primary source.

questions.question: If a source was created 500 years AFTER the event it describes, it is most likely what?
questions.explanation: A source made long after the event is a secondary source.

questions.question: Which statement about primary and secondary sources is TRUE?

choices.A: Primary sources are firsthand; secondary sources are made later
choices.B: Secondary sources always come from the event itself
choices.D: There is no difference between the two

questions.explanation: Primary sources are firsthand, while secondary sources are made later by people studying the past.

questions.question: A historian reads an ancient diary, then checks a modern textbook. Why use the textbook too?

choices.B: To understand what experts think the diary means
choices.C: Because the diary cannot be trusted

questions.explanation: The secondary textbook helps the historian understand what experts think the primary diary means.

1-3.title: How Historians and Geographers Investigate
1-3.learn:
KEY IDEAS — INVESTIGATING THE PAST AND PLACE

Historical inquiry means asking questions about the past and hunting for evidence to answer them, almost like a detective. Historians gather sources, compare them, and look for agreement or differences. They quickly notice that two people can describe the SAME event in different ways, so they check multiple sources before deciding what likely happened. This careful checking is called corroboration.

Geographers study WHERE events happened and why place matters. They use the five themes of geography: location (where something is), place (what it is like), human-environment interaction (how people and nature affect each other), movement (of people, goods, and ideas), and region (areas with shared features). Tools like maps and globes help them. Lines called latitude (run east-west) and longitude (run north-south) help pinpoint any spot on Earth.

Together, historians and geographers show that both TIME and PLACE shape history. Where a civilization grew — near a river, on an island, in a desert — often explains how it lived and grew.

questions.question: What does 'historical inquiry' mean?

choices.B: Memorizing every date in a book
choices.D: Asking questions about the past and looking for evidence

questions.explanation: Historical inquiry is investigating the past by asking questions and gathering evidence.

questions.question: Why do historians compare more than one source about an event?

choices.B: Because two people may describe the same event differently
choices.C: Because they want more pages to read

questions.explanation: Different witnesses can describe the same event differently, so historians compare sources.

questions.question: What do geographers mainly study?

choices.A: Where things are and why place matters

questions.explanation: Geographers study location and how place shapes events and people.

questions.question: Which is one of the five themes of geography?
questions.explanation: Movement is one of the five themes, along with location, place, region, and human-environment interaction.

questions.question: Lines of latitude and longitude are used to do what?

choices.A: Pinpoint an exact location on Earth
choices.B: Tell the year of an event

questions.explanation: Latitude and longitude lines let you locate any exact spot on the globe.

questions.question: Comparing sources to see if they back each other up is a way historians do what?

choices.B: Check how trustworthy the evidence is
choices.C: Decide which source is the prettiest

questions.explanation: Cross-checking sources helps historians judge whether evidence is reliable.

questions.question: Why might WHERE a civilization grew (such as near a river) matter to historians?

choices.B: Place often explains how a civilization lived and grew
choices.C: Rivers have nothing to do with farming

questions.explanation: Geography, like nearby rivers, often shapes how a civilization survives and grows.

questions.question: A historian acting 'like a detective' is mostly doing what?
questions.explanation: Like a detective, a historian collects clues (sources) and weighs the evidence.

questions.question: Which tool would a geographer MOST likely use?
questions.explanation: Geographers use maps and globes to study location and place.

questions.question: Two ancient writers describe a battle differently. What should a careful historian do?

choices.A: Compare both accounts and look for more evidence before deciding

questions.explanation: A historian corroborates by comparing accounts and seeking more evidence.

questions.question: What is the name for checking several sources against each other to see if they agree?
questions.explanation: Comparing sources to see if they back each other up is called corroboration.

questions.question: Which of these is one of the five themes of geography?
questions.explanation: Location is one of the five themes of geography.

questions.question: Lines of latitude run in which direction?
questions.explanation: Lines of latitude run east-west.

questions.question: Lines of longitude run in which direction?
questions.explanation: Lines of longitude run north-south.

questions.question: The geography theme that describes how people and nature affect each other is called what?
questions.explanation: Human-environment interaction describes how people and nature affect each other.

questions.question: An area of land with shared features, such as a desert region, fits which geography theme?
questions.explanation: Region is the theme that describes areas with shared features.

questions.question: The movement of people, goods, and ideas from place to place fits which geography theme?
questions.explanation: Movement is the theme about people, goods, and ideas traveling from place to place.

questions.question: Why might two eyewitnesses describe the same event in different ways?

choices.D: Because people notice and remember different details

questions.explanation: People notice and remember different details, so accounts of the same event can differ.

questions.question: A historian who keeps asking questions and hunting for evidence is using a skill most like that of a what?
questions.explanation: Asking questions and gathering clues makes a historian work much like a detective.

questions.question: Which tool helps a geographer see the whole round Earth at once?
questions.explanation: A globe is a round model that shows the whole Earth at once.

questions.question: How does a civilization built next to a river often benefit?

choices.C: It gets water for drinking and farming
choices.D: It is cut off from everyone

questions.explanation: A river provides water for drinking and farming, helping a civilization grow.

questions.question: Together, what do historians and geographers show shapes history?
questions.explanation: Historians and geographers show that both time and place shape history.

questions.question: What is the FIRST step in historical inquiry?

choices.A: Asking a question about the past
choices.D: Drawing a picture of the future

questions.explanation: Historical inquiry begins by asking a question about the past.

questions.question: Which is NOT one of the five themes of geography?
questions.explanation: Multiplication is a math skill, not one of the five themes of geography.

questions.question: Using both latitude and longitude lines together lets you do what?

choices.A: Tell the exact year of an event
choices.B: Pinpoint any exact spot on Earth
choices.C: Find out who won a war
choices.D: Measure how heavy a mountain is

questions.explanation: Latitude and longitude crossing together pinpoint any exact spot on Earth.

questions.question: Why is comparing several sources better than trusting just one?

choices.A: One source might be incomplete or mistaken
choices.C: It saves the historian from thinking

questions.explanation: A single source might be incomplete or mistaken, so historians compare several.

questions.question: The geography theme 'place' describes what about an area?

choices.C: What the area is like, its features

questions.explanation: The theme of place describes what an area is like, its physical and human features.

questions.question: A civilization in a dry desert would MOST need to solve which problem to survive?
questions.explanation: In a dry desert, finding enough water would be the biggest challenge to survival.

questions.question: An island civilization would MOST likely become skilled at what because of its location?

choices.D: Sailing and fishing on the sea

questions.explanation: Surrounded by water, an island people would most likely become skilled at sailing and fishing.

questions.question: Which question is an example of historical inquiry?

choices.A: Why did this ancient city build walls?
choices.C: How many cookies are in the jar?

questions.explanation: Asking why an ancient city built walls is a historical-inquiry question about the past.

questions.question: A geographer asking 'Where exactly is this city?' is focusing on which theme?
questions.explanation: Asking where something is focuses on the theme of location.

questions.question: A geographer studies how farmers built canals to bring river water to their fields. Which theme is this?
questions.explanation: Building canals shows people and nature affecting each other, the theme of human-environment interaction.

questions.question: What should a historian do if two reliable sources disagree about an event?

choices.A: Pick one at random and ignore the other
choices.D: Look for more evidence before deciding

questions.explanation: When sources disagree, a careful historian looks for more evidence before deciding.

questions.question: Studying the movement of traders along a road between two empires fits which geography theme?
questions.explanation: Traders traveling along a road is an example of the movement theme.

questions.question: Both historians and geographers help us understand the past by studying what two things?
questions.explanation: Historians study time and geographers study place; together they explain the past.

questions.question: Why is it useful to know WHERE a civilization was located?

choices.A: Location has no effect on people
choices.B: It can explain how the people farmed, traveled, and traded
choices.C: It only matters for drawing maps
choices.D: It tells you nothing about their lives

questions.explanation: A civilization's location can explain how its people farmed, traveled, and traded.

questions.question: What does a map mainly help a geographer understand?

choices.A: The exact year a battle happened
choices.C: Where places are and how they relate to each other

questions.explanation: A map shows where places are and how they relate to one another.

questions.question: A historian reads one diary and stops there. What is the main problem with this?

choices.B: One source may give an incomplete or one-sided view
choices.D: There is no problem at all

questions.explanation: Relying on just one source may give an incomplete or one-sided view of events.

questions.question: Which pairing correctly matches a worker to what they study?

choices.A: Geographer studies place; historian studies time and the past
choices.B: Historian studies maps only; geographer studies dates only

questions.explanation: A geographer studies place, while a historian studies time and the past.

questions.question: Which activity best shows a geographer at work?

choices.C: Using a map to study where a city sits and why

questions.explanation: Using a map to study where a city sits and why shows a geographer at work.
